title: Personal error log
summary: Use evidence from several attempts to select two recurring, high-value error patterns and apply a precise correction-and-retest routine.

sections.title: Turn mistakes into evidence
content: One incorrect answer is an event; a recurring error is a pattern supported by more than one attempt. A useful error log records enough evidence to distinguish the two. It does not label a learner as ‘bad at grammar’ or ‘careless’. It names an observable choice that can be checked and changed.

Collect the task, the exact error, the corrected form and the reason for the correction. Compare entries across different days or task types. A pattern becomes a priority when it recurs, damages meaning or accuracy, and has a correction routine the learner can actually apply.

sections.title: Name the pattern precisely
content: Replace vague labels with testable descriptions. ‘Punctuation problem’ becomes ‘I join two independent clauses with only a comma.’ ‘My conclusions are too strong’ becomes ‘I use absolute words such as every, always or proves when the evidence covers a limited group or period.’ Each precise name points towards a check.

Keep examples with the label. The sentence ‘The trial was short, it produced useful observations’ contains two complete clauses joined by a comma. Its correction may use a full stop, semicolon or suitable conjunction. The example prevents the rule from becoming an empty slogan.

sections.title: Choose two high-value priorities
content: Count recurrence, then judge impact and actionability. An error repeated three times is stronger evidence than a single slip. An unsupported universal claim may occur only twice but still deserves attention because it changes the truth of the response. A rare spelling mistake may remain in the record without becoming an active priority.

Work on no more than two patterns at once. A long list divides attention and makes improvement hard to measure. Keep other entries as evidence, but promote them only when a current pattern improves or new attempts show that another problem has become more important.

sections.title: Build a short correction routine
content: Use five moves: Notice, Name, Correct, Check, Retest. Notice the trigger in a real sentence. Name the exact pattern. Correct the sentence without changing its intended meaning. Check it with one specific question. Retest the same skill on a fresh sentence or task rather than merely rereading the answer.

For comma splices, the check might be: ‘Are there complete clauses on both sides of this comma?’ For overclaiming, it might be: ‘Do words such as all, always, never or proves travel beyond the measured group, place, time or outcome?’ A check must be short enough to use independently.

sections.title: Retest and record the result
content: A corrected old answer shows that feedback was understood; a correct new answer shows transfer. After practising the routine, complete a fresh item without looking at the model. Record whether the pattern was avoided, caught during checking or noticed only after feedback.

Use several later attempts before claiming that a pattern is resolved. If the error returns, adjust the cue or routine rather than writing ‘be more careful’. The log should change future behaviour: what to notice, what question to ask and what evidence will show improvement.

sections.title: Keep the log honest and useful
content: Do not invent a weakness from one difficult question or copy another learner's priorities. Do not count the same underlying error twice under different labels. Link every pattern to dated examples, preserve the corrected meaning and distinguish an independently corrected error from one fixed only after feedback.

Review the active pair regularly: retain a pattern if evidence still shows it, retire it after repeated successful transfer, or replace it when another recurring error has greater impact. The goal is not a permanent record of failure; it is a small decision tool for the next practice session.

sections.title: Build a two-pattern action plan
content: Analyse an original eight-entry review log. Identify the evidence for recurrence, choose two high-value patterns, name each precisely, attach a correction check and select a one-week retest plan. Complete all six decisions before viewing feedback.
